strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 8+ safety benchmarks with consistent improvements (0.138 vs 0.478 ASR on WG:Test, 65.5% improvement on WildJailBreak)
Well-motivated shift from reactive to proactive safety training through dynamic co-evolution with game-theoretic grounding
Novel hidden CoT mechanism enabling asymmetric strategic planning, demonstrating +45.3% attack diversity improvement
Rigorous diversity analysis using both Self-BLEU and SBERT metrics, with effective t-SNE visualization of attack clustering
Strong ablation studies (Self-Play, Self-Play+SFT, Self-Play(No CoT), Attacker-Only, Defender-Only) isolating contribution of each component
Detailed experimental reproducibility with comprehensive hyperparameters, computational requirements (10-15 hours), and promised code release
Honest treatment of limitations and emergent safety properties from parameter sharing
Preservation of general capabilities (minimal degradation on AlpacaEval-2, IFEval, reasoning benchmarks)
Clear algorithmic presentation (Algorithm 1) and practical implementation using Re++ with practical design choices
weaknesses: Theorem 1 assumes unrealistic Nash Equilibrium convergence with no evidence training approaches NE; theoretical safety guarantee is largely vacuous in practice
Limited baseline comparisons—primarily compares against own baselines rather than SOTA safety methods (Constitutional AI, SafeRLHF, DPO approaches, Ma et al. [36])
Single-turn evaluation only despite claiming framework supports multi-turn; real jailbreaks often use multi-turn interactions making generalization unclear
Heavy reliance on WildGuard-7B reward model without sensitivity analysis or investigation of systematic biases; circular evaluation concern using same model for training and testing
Hidden CoT mechanism effectiveness empirically demonstrated but mechanistic understanding lacking—unclear whether improvements stem from privacy, reasoning structure, or strategic behavior emergence
Starting from abliterated (safety-alignment-removed) model is non-standard; limited justification beyond computational efficiency and makes comparison to standard safety-aligned baselines problematic
Only Llama-3.1-8B tested; generalization to other model families (Qwen, etc.) and larger models unclear despite claims of broader applicability
Diversity metrics limited to automatic measures (Self-BLEU, SBERT); manual evaluation of attack quality and semantic diversity would strengthen claims

Over-claimed novelty—self-play, parameter sharing, and Re++ algorithm are from prior work; 'first scalable online MARL for LM safety' claim needs stronger differentiation from prior work (SPAG, SPIN, Ma et al.)
Safeguards against dual-use risks incomplete—emergent safety only occurs <10% of cases and external safeguards (Appendix D) lack empirical validation of effectiveness
SFT dataset self-distillation process could introduce distribution shift and potential artifacts from using abliterated model for data generation
Potentially non-standard advantage normalization per role (Eq. 2) in zero-sum setting lacks analysis of interaction with game structure

strengths: Novel game-theoretic formulation of LM safety as co-evolving attacker-defender roles, addressing real limitations of reactive sequential approaches

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple safety benchmarks (WildGuard, WildJailBreak, HarmBench, DAN, XSTest, OR-Bench, STRONGREJECT) with strong safety improvements (0.138 vs 0.478 ASR on WG:Test)
Hidden Chain-of-Thought mechanism elegantly encourages attack diversity (+45.3% SBERT) while reducing over-refusal through asymmetric private reasoning
Clear empirical demonstration that self-play generates more diverse attacks than training against static defenders, with effective t-SNE visualizations and quantitative analysis
Detailed experimental documentation and reproducibility information including hyperparameters, dataset construction, and implementation details
Theoretical grounding via game-theoretic framework and Nash Equilibrium analysis motivates the approach
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is straightforward (NE ⟹ safe) with simple proof; assumes perfect reward model and unrealistic conditions (naive refusal gets zero reward); lacks convergence analysis or connection between theory and empirical practice

Significant capability degradation: AlpacaEval-2 drops 45.4% for Self-play (19.22→10.51%) and 15.1% even with SFT (16.34%); Llama models degrade 2-3× more than Qwen models, raising generalizability concerns

Narrow experimental scope in main paper: single model family (Llama-3.1-8B-abliterated); multi-model results (Qwen, Llama-3.1-8B-IT) relegated to preliminary Appendix A with concerning timing ('August 2025'); only single-turn interactions evaluated in main results
No empirical evidence that training converges to Nash Equilibrium; Figure 3 shows ongoing adaptation rather than equilibrium, undermining the theoretical guarantee's relevance

Entire framework depends on WildGuard-7B reward model with no sensitivity analysis, cross-model validation, robustness testing, or validation that reward labels align with true safety; circular reasoning risk if reward model has systematic biases
Use of abliterated (unaligned) starting model is artificial; doesn't reflect typical safety alignment which builds on already-safe models; sidesteps the core challenge of fine-tuning aligned models
Auxiliary SFT regularization (Eq. 4) appears ad-hoc rather than principled solution to capability degradation, suggesting fundamental tension between RL objective and general capabilities
Active backdoor risk dismissed too lightly; emergent internal safeguard occurs in <10% of checkpoints (unreliable); proposed safeguards in Appendix E lack demonstration of effectiveness
Computational efficiency not addressed: 10-15 hours on 4 A100-80GB GPUs for ~300 steps with no cost comparison to baselines; inference requires both components (doubled cost)
Limited failure analysis: no systematic examination of which attack types remain undetected, remaining vulnerabilities, or out-of-distribution robustness despite diversity gains
Multi-turn attack evaluation underdeveloped (only Appendix A.3, 9-44% improvements); single-turn training with claimed multi-turn transferability needs stronger validation

Missing critical ablations: reward model choice sensitivity, impact of parameter sharing removal, contribution of individual reward shaping terms; high variance in some metrics (Fig 3d) without statistical significance testing

strengths: Novel end-to-end online MARL framework for full-parameter LM safety training, the first to achieve this at scale without significant quantization
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 10+ safety benchmarks with proper baselines, 8 runs, and confidence intervals
Key empirical finding: co-evolution maintains attack diversity (+21.8% SBERT), while static-defender baselines converge to dominant attack modes
Clever technical contribution with Hidden CoT mechanism enabling asymmetric strategic planning and improved attack diversity (+45.3%)
Strong safety improvements on multiple benchmarks (0.138 vs. 0.478 ASR on WG:Test; robust performance on WildJailBreak, DAN, HarmBench)
Well-motivated problem: shifts from reactive patching to proactive co-evolution, addressing fundamental limitations of existing approaches
Principled game-theoretic framework with safety guarantee (Theorem 1) providing theoretical justification
Honest limitations discussion and thoughtful safety considerations (Appendices D, E with deployment safeguards)
weaknesses: Significant gap between theory and practice: Theorem 1 assumes convergence to Nash Equilibrium and relies on strong assumptions (reward model accuracy, refusal receives r=0); no convergence analysis or empirical verification of NE proximity
Concerning capability degradation on general benchmarks: AlpacaEval-2 drops 15% (19.22→16.34), IFEval drops 20%; SFT recovery is incomplete, raising unresolved safety-capability trade-off questions

Limited experimental scope: primary results only on Llama-3.1-8B; Appendix A contains preliminary results on other models (Qwen 3B/7B/14B) marked as future work, raising concerns about cherry-picking or incomplete evaluation

Reward function design under-explored: four components with no ablation studies on individual reward contributions; sensitivity to hyperparameters not analyzed; no comparison of alternative reward models
Critical dependency on reward model correctness: entire framework assumes WildGuard-7B accurately judges harmfulness; no analysis of failure modes or error propagation
Single-turn evaluation only: multi-turn attack generalization untested despite acknowledged importance; transferability results (Appendix A.3) show variable success
Missing ablations: no analysis of individual reward function components, CoT format variations, or hyperparameter sensitivity despite adding multiple design choices
Parameter sharing creates non-deterministic emergent behavior: attackers occasionally refuse generation (~10% of checkpoints, Table 8); unclear if beneficial
High variance in results: Figure 4 bootstrapped distributions show substantial overlap with baselines on some metrics
Presentation issue: Appendix A announces 'major revision' with 'significantly stronger' results but calls them 'preliminary,' creating uncertainty about work completion and result selection
